original_question: Determine the number of lozenge tilings of a regular hexagon after removing two innermost unit triangles, one upward-pointing and one downward-pointing. Account for the two geometrically distinct placements in which the removed triangles are opposite or adjacent.
target_in_paper: Section 2 ("Lozenges"), Problem 4: determine the number of lozenge tilings of a regular hexagon after removing one upward-pointing and one downward-pointing innermost unit triangle; the immediately preceding paragraph specifies that, among the six central triangles, there are exactly two symmetry classes for such a pair, namely opposite and adjacent. ([faculty.uml.edu](https://faculty.uml.edu/jpropp/matchings.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper's exact target: it has the correct region (a regular hexagon), the correct defect pattern (two innermost unit triangles, one upward-pointing and one downward-pointing), and the correct split into the two geometrically distinct central placements, opposite and adjacent. ([faculty.uml.edu](https://faculty.uml.edu/jpropp/matchings.pdf))
missing_details: The side-length parameter is implicit in the draft. To be fully stand-alone, the region should be specified as the n,n,n,n,n,n semiregular hexagon (equivalently, a regular hexagon of side length n), and the question should ask for the count as a function of n. ([faculty.uml.edu](https://faculty.uml.edu/jpropp/matchings.pdf))

The ambient lattice/model should be stated explicitly: the hexagon is dissected into unit equilateral triangles in the triangular lattice, and a lozenge is the union of two adjacent unit triangles. ([faculty.uml.edu](https://faculty.uml.edu/jpropp/matchings.pdf))

The removed triangles are not arbitrary interior triangles; they are chosen from the six central ("innermost") unit triangles of the regular hexagon. ([faculty.uml.edu](https://faculty.uml.edu/jpropp/matchings.pdf))

The two placements are meant up to symmetry: the chosen upward-pointing and downward-pointing central triangles are either opposite or adjacent. ([faculty.uml.edu](https://faculty.uml.edu/jpropp/matchings.pdf))

To match the paper's intent precisely, the question should ask for the exact enumeration in each of the two cases, not merely mention that both cases should be considered. ([faculty.uml.edu](https://faculty.uml.edu/jpropp/matchings.pdf))
refined_question: For each integer n >= 1, let H_n be the regular hexagon of side length n on the triangular lattice (equivalently, the n,n,n,n,n,n semiregular hexagon), and let a lozenge be the union of two adjacent unit equilateral triangles. Among the six central unit triangles of H_n, remove one upward-pointing triangle and one downward-pointing triangle. Up to symmetry there are exactly two cases: the removed central triangles are opposite, or they are adjacent. Determine, for each n, the exact number of lozenge tilings of the resulting region in each case. ([faculty.uml.edu](https://faculty.uml.edu/jpropp/matchings.pdf))
justification: This is the narrowest paper-faithful stand-alone version of the draft. Section 2 first defines lozenges and semiregular hexagons, then specializes to a=b=c and explains that the six central triangles yield exactly two symmetry types of an upward/downward pair, opposite and adjacent; Problem 4 then asks for the tiling count of the resulting regular-hexagon regions. The rewrite therefore adds only the implicit parameter n and the lattice/lozenge definitions needed for self-containment, while avoiding any broader shift to off-center holes or to the more general asymmetric hexagons treated in the progress discussion. No ambient ring/field, operator, homogeneity, degree, nilpotency, or "sufficiently large" condition is relevant here, because the problem is purely enumerative-combinatorial. ([faculty.uml.edu](https://faculty.uml.edu/jpropp/matchings.pdf))
